title: 3.5.26 Objects and Properties
description: Eight multiple-choice questions on object literals, dot vs bracket access, nesting, methods, options objects, and destructuring. Checked instantly.

questions.question: You need to store a name, an age and a city for one student as a single value. Which shape fits best?
options: An array, because there are three values
An object literal with a key for each fact
Three separate variables with matching name prefixes
A string that joins the three values with commas
questions.explanation: An object answers "which name?" and groups different facts about one thing. An array answers "which position?" and is for interchangeable items of the same kind.

questions.question: A student writes console.log(car.model) on an object that has no `model` property. What happens?
options: It throws a ReferenceError
It throws a TypeError
It prints undefined
It creates the property and prints null
questions.explanation: Reading a property that does not exist gives undefined rather than an error. An undeclared variable is what throws a ReferenceError; a missing property fails silently.

questions.question: An object `book` already has a `pages` property. What does the line `book.pages = 480;` do?
options: Creates a second `pages` property
Changes the value of the existing `pages` property
Deletes `pages` and replaces the whole object
Fails, because `book` was declared with const
questions.explanation: Assignment to an existing property overwrites it, and it works even when the object was declared with const (const stops rebinding the variable, not changing the object). Assigning to a name that is not there would create a new property.

questions.question: Given const key = "price"; and const item = { price: 10 };, what does item.key give and what does item[key] give?
options: Both give 10
item.key gives 10; item[key] gives undefined
item.key gives undefined; item[key] gives 10
Both give undefined
questions.explanation: Dot notation looks for a property literally named `key`, which does not exist, so item.key is undefined. Square brackets evaluate the variable first, find "price", and fetch that property, giving 10.

questions.question: Which property can NOT be reached with dot notation, so brackets are required?
options: A property whose key contains a space, such as "font size"
A property whose value is a number
A property whose value is a boolean
A property that is the last one in the object literal
questions.explanation: Dot notation needs a name that is a single typeable word, so a key with a space in it can only be reached with brackets. The value's type and the property's position make no difference.

questions.question: Given const student = { address: { city: "Chico" } };, which expression reads the city?
options: student[address.city]
student.address[city]
student.address.city
student[address][city]
questions.explanation: Read the chain left to right: take student, get its address object, then get that object's city. Each step is the same dot operation applied to whatever the previous step produced.

questions.question: What is the difference between word.toUpperCase and word.toUpperCase()?
options: Nothing; the parentheses are optional
The first is an error; the second runs
The first is the function value itself; the second calls it and gives the result
The first changes the string; the second only reads it
questions.explanation: A method is a property whose value is a function. Without parentheses you get the function itself; with them you call it and get its return value. The same rule that applies to any function value.

questions.question: Why is passing one options object often safer than passing four positional arguments?
options: It runs faster than four arguments
Each value carries its name, so keys decide placement and order cannot silently swap values
It is the only way to pass more than one value to a function
Positional arguments cannot be used with functions that return a value
questions.explanation: With positional arguments, two same-typed values can be swapped and nothing errors. An options object attaches each name to its value, so the keys, not the order, determine what goes where.
